name: Sturgeon's Law
statement: Ninety percent of everything is crap.
meaning: In any field, the vast majority of what is produced is mediocre, and that is normal, not a sign the field is worthless.
mechanism: Quality is hard and rare; most output clusters near the average, with only a thin top slice of excellence. Judging a whole field by its bulk is therefore misleading, because the bulk of anything (books, music, science, startups) is unremarkable almost by definition. The exceptional is, always, the exception.

examples.text: The saying was born defending science fiction: critics judged the whole genre by its pulpiest work, and Sturgeon's retort was that of course most SF is dross (so is most of every genre) and the best SF stands with the best writing anywhere.

The flood of forgettable films or streaming tracks in any year does not indict cinema or music as forms. You judge a medium by its masterpieces, not its multiplex average; every catalogue is mostly filler.

As barriers to publishing collapse (self-published books, app stores, social feeds) the visible volume of weak work balloons and seems to 'prove' the 90%. But the ratio of excellent to mediocre is roughly constant across eras; only the raw quantity changed.

variants.name: Sturgeon's Law proper
variants.text: Confusingly, Sturgeon called the '90%' line his Revelation. His actual 'Law' was a different sentence, 'Nothing is always absolutely so', a caution against absolutes. Popular usage (and the OED) collapsed the Revelation into the Law, which is now the dominant sense.

whyItMatters: It is a defence against cherry-picking: you cannot damn a whole category by its worst examples, because ninety percent of every category is weak. It reframes evaluation around the top of the distribution rather than the mass.

working.lead: Judge a field by its best
working.text: the top slice is what a category is capable of; the average is just the base rate of mediocrity, which is universal.

working.lead: Don't damn a category by its worst
working.text: pointing at the dross proves nothing distinctive: every field has a 90%, so the worst examples are not evidence against the field.

working.lead: Expect volume to rise, not quality
working.text: when barriers fall, the trash grows fastest and most visibly; that is the ratio holding, not the field decaying.
'90%' is a vivid figure, never a measurement: use it to resist unfair dismissal, not as a statistic.

limits: The '90%' is invented rhetoric with no study behind it, so it should never be cited as a statistic. 'Crap' (Sturgeon's own word was 'crud') is a subjective judgement that varies by taste, era, and expertise, which makes the boundary undefinable. And the aphorism cuts both ways as an excuse: it can wave away legitimate criticism of genuinely poor work ('well, 90% of everything is crap') just as easily as it defends a field from unfair attack. There is even a terminological muddle at its root — using 'Sturgeon's Law' for the 90% idea is technically a misnomer, though now standard.
misreadings: The '90%' is rhetorical, not a measurement, and 'crap' means mediocre, not evil. It is not cynicism or a claim that nothing is good. It is the opposite, a case for judging things by their finest work rather than their most abundant.
origin: Coined by the science-fiction author Theodore Sturgeon, who called it his 'Revelation' while defending the genre against critics who cited its worst work. He aired the idea in a lecture around 1951 and at the 1953 World Science Fiction Convention in Philadelphia, and set it in print in his Venture Science Fiction column: the '90% of everything is crud' formulation with its two corollaries appearing in March 1958. His original word was 'crud', not 'crap'.

sources.text: Sturgeon, T. (March 1958). Book column, Venture Science Fiction. — the 'Sturgeon's Revelation' passage with its two corollaries.
Sturgeon's law, Wikipedia. — the Revelation-versus-Law distinction, the 1951/1953/1958 timeline, and the 'crud'/'crap' wording.
